title: Sfogliatelle ricotta
subtitle: Neapolitan shell pastry with sweetened ricotta filling
excerpt: Sfogliatelle are Neapolitan shell-shaped pastries built from an extremely thin, almost transparent dough that is stretched, rolled into a log, then sliced and shaped into cones. You get hundreds of paper-thin crisp layers on the outside and a dense, fragrant ricotta and semolina filling inside. Watch the dough during stretching: any tearing creates gaps where the layers fuse during baking and the shell loses its characteristic flaky shatter.
sourceNotes: Sfogliatelle originate from the Neapolitan pastry tradition, with documented recipes from the 18th century. The ricce (curly) version uses the stretched, layered pastry described here. The filling of ricotta, semolina, and candied peel is the classic Neapolitan standard.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the filling up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate. The shaped pastry log can be refrigerated overnight before slicing. Baked sfogliatelle are best eaten on the day they are made.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until the layers are a deep golden amber and the shells feel rigid when tapped.

glossaryTerms.definition: Neapolitan shell-shaped pastries (singular: sfogliatella) made from very thin layered dough. Sfogliatelle ricce (curly) uses a stretched, rolled, and re-sliced dough to create the characteristic hundreds of fine layers. Sfogliatelle frolle uses short pastry instead, and is much easier to make. Ricce are defined by their layered shell texture.

The technique of creating many thin alternating layers in a dough or pastry. In sfogliatelle the lamination is achieved by stretching the dough extremely thin, coating it with lard or butter, rolling it into a tight log, and then slicing the log to expose the wound layers. Each slice is opened out by pressing the centre to form a cone.

Coarsely ground durum wheat with a pale yellow colour and a slightly gritty texture. In the sfogliatelle filling, semolina is cooked into a very thick porridge with milk, which then sets firm on cooling. It provides structure to the filling so that it holds its shape inside the pastry shell during baking.

content.text: Sfogliatelle are Neapolitan shell pastries formed by stretching a stiff dough to near transparency, coating it with fat, rolling it into a log, slicing the log into rounds, and pressing each round into a cone shape before filling, a process that produces the characteristic

content.text: Method
Making the pastry dough

Combine the flour, salt, and honey in a large bowl. Add the lukewarm water gradually, mixing with your hands until a stiff, cohesive dough forms. It should feel noticeably stiffer and drier than bread dough; this is intentional. A stiff dough stretches without tearing as easily as a soft one and creates a crisper shell.

Knead the dough firmly for 10 full minutes. The dough will be tough at first and may feel almost unyielding. Keep working it: by 8 to 10 minutes it should feel smooth, elastic, and only slightly tacky. The gluten development from this kneading is what allows the dough to stretch to near transparency without tearing.
Wrap the dough tightly in cling film and rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. This resting period relaxes the gluten so the dough stretches rather than springing back. Do not skip this rest.
Stretching and rolling the pastry

This stage requires space: a large table or counter is essential. Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. Work with one piece at a time, keeping the rest wrapped. On a lightly floured surface, roll one piece into a rectangle as thin as you can get it with a rolling pin. The dough will spring back; work patiently, rolling from the centre outward, letting the dough rest for 30 seconds between passes if it resists.

Once the rolling pin cannot make the dough thinner, switch to hand-stretching. Drape the dough over the backs of both hands and gently pull outward from the centre, working around the sheet, allowing gravity to stretch it. The goal is a sheet about 60 to 70 cm long and nearly transparent: you should be able to read text through it. Small holes are acceptable; large tears require patching by overlapping the torn edges by 1 cm.

Lay the stretched sheet flat on the table. Using a pastry brush, coat the entire surface with a thin, even layer of softened lard or butter. Work quickly; the dough dries out if left uncovered too long.

Starting from one short edge, roll the sheet into a tight log, as you would roll a Swiss roll but applying firm pressure as you go to compact the layers. The log should be as tight as possible. Repeat with the remaining 3 pieces of dough, each time rolling the new sheet and buttering it, then continuing the log from where the previous piece ended, building one long log. Wrap the finished log in cling film and refrigerate for at least 1 hour (or overnight). The chilling firms the fat so the slices hold their shape when cut.
Making the filling

Pour the milk into a medium saucepan and bring to a simmer over medium heat. Add the semolina in a thin, steady stream, whisking constantly. Cook over low heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring continuously, until the mixture is extremely thick and pulls away from the sides of the pan. Spread onto a plate or baking sheet, press cling film onto the surface, and refrigerate until completely cold and set firm.

Once the semolina is cold and firm, break it into chunks and place in a large bowl with the ricotta, icing sugar, eggs, vanilla extract, candied peel, and cinnamon. Beat everything together firmly until well combined. The filling should be thick and hold its shape when scooped. If it is too loose (from a very wet ricotta), refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm up.
Slicing, shaping, and filling
Heat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius (conventional). Line two baking trays with baking mats or parchment.
Remove the log from the refrigerator. Using a sharp knife, cut the log into rounds about 1.5 cm thick. You should get 12 rounds. The cut ends will show a spiral cross-section of pastry layers.

Working with one round at a time, place it flat on the table. Using both thumbs pressed into the centre of the round and working in a rotating motion, gently press and open the centre outward to form a small cone or cup shape. The layers will fan out around the opening. The cone should be deep enough to hold 2 to 3 tablespoons of filling. If the pastry cracks as you shape it, warm the round briefly between your palms and try again.

Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of filling into the cone. Gently pinch the open edge together to partially enclose the filling; do not press hard enough to merge the layers. Place on the lined baking tray. Repeat with all 12 rounds.
Baking
Brush the outside of each pastry with a little softened lard or melted butter using the pastry brush. This helps the outer layers brown and gives a glossy finish.

Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until the layers are a deep golden amber throughout and the shells feel rigid when tapped on the underside. The layered edges should be deeply coloured; pale sfogliatelle will be chewy and soft rather than shatteringly crisp. Transfer to a cooling rack for 5 minutes, then dust generously with icing sugar and serve warm.

attrs.problem: The pastry layers did not separate during baking and the shell is chewy rather than crisp
attrs.avoid: Avoid applying too much fat between the layers: a thin, even coat allows the layers to separate as steam forms; too thick a layer glues them together.
attrs.fix: The dough may also not have been stretched thin enough. Each layer must be near-transparent before rolling. Thick layers fuse more easily and produce less dramatic separation.

attrs.problem: The filling leaked out during baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid overfilling the cones. A maximum of 3 tablespoons per pastry is enough; above this the filling cannot be adequately contained by the open edge.
attrs.fix: The filling may also be too loose. Drain the ricotta through a fine sieve for a full hour before using, and make sure the semolina porridge was cooked until very stiff.

attrs.problem: The pastry log crumbled or broke apart when slicing
attrs.avoid: Avoid slicing the log before it has been refrigerated for at least 1 hour. The fat must be fully solid to hold the layers together during cutting.
attrs.fix: Use the sharpest knife available and cut with a single decisive downward motion rather than sawing. A sawing motion drags the layers and causes the log to unravel.

attrs.problem: The dough kept tearing during hand-stretching
attrs.avoid: Avoid stretching too aggressively in one spot. Move around the sheet, working gradually, to distribute the stretching evenly.
attrs.fix: The dough may need more resting time. Cover with a damp cloth for 10 minutes and try again. If the dough was not kneaded for long enough, it will lack elasticity and resist stretching.
